summary: This informational document is a product of the Path Aware Networking Research Group. It catalogs and analyzes earlier attempts to develop and deploy path aware networking techniques, most of which were unsuccessful or only partly successful, to draw lessons for researchers working on such systems today.

eli5.summary: Sometimes you want to pick your own road across the Internet instead of letting the map choose. This document looks at many past tries at that, explains why most did not catch on, and shares lessons.

questions: obstacles to deploying path aware networking
why did path aware networking fail
subtitle: Why decades of attempts to let apps choose network paths have mostly failed

tldr.problem: Applications often send traffic over inefficient paths; many approaches have tried to let endpoints pick or steer their routes, with limited success.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs past path-aware proposals (from the 1980s onward), analyzes why each failed or saw limited adoption, and extracts lessons for future research.
tldr.outcome: The research group identified 13 lessons, from deployment economics to trust models, that apply to any path-aware technique.

facts.label: Lessons extracted
facts.value: 13 lessons, covering deployment, economics, trust, and operations

today: RFC 9049 is an informational document from the IRTF Path Aware Networking Research Group. It serves as a cautionary reference for protocol designers and researchers working on any future technique that would involve endpoints making path-aware decisions.

sections.title: The Problem and the Question
sections.content:
Path Aware Networking describes the ability for endpoints to discover properties of network paths they use (latency, loss, available bandwidth) and to react by selecting different paths or changing how they send data. The Internet community has experimented with this for decades, starting with Stream Transport (ST) in the late 1970s. Yet most path-aware techniques have seen limited or no deployment.

The Path Aware Networking Research Group set out to catalog these attempts and understand why they failed. This RFC is the result: a bestiary of roads not taken, with analysis of the obstacles that prevented success.
sections.eli5: Engineers have tried many times to let applications talk directly to the network about which path to take. Almost none of these ideas caught on. This document explains why.

sections.title: Patterns in the Failures
sections.content:
The RFC examines nine major path-aware techniques: Stream Transport (ST/ST2), Integrated Services (IntServ), Quick-Start TCP, ICMP Source Quench, Triggers for Transport (TRIGTRAN), Shim6, Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS), IPv6 Flow Labels, and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN). For each, it documents the original problem, how the approach worked, and why it did not succeed broadly.

The research group developed a framework of 13 lessons learned, organized by category: economic factors (justifying deployment, paying for new techniques), architectural challenges (deployment incrementally, state management), trust (endpoints trusting intermediate nodes, and vice versa), and operational concerns (changes required to networks and protocol stacks).
sections.eli5: Nine different attempts, each addressing real problems, each hitting different walls. The walls themselves turned out to be more interesting than any single technical solution.

sections.title: Economics and Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
A key lesson: the benefit of a path-aware technique must be great enough to justify the cost and risk of network upgrades. Operators use the principle 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it.' IntServ required every router on a path to be upgraded and to maintain per-flow state for admission control. Yet between 1994 and 2000, Internet capacity increased so dramatically (from 45 Mbps to 2.4 Gbps) that QoS simply became unnecessary; operators could solve the problem by adding bandwidth.

Early adopters matter. If a technique only works when everyone deploys it, adoption stalls. Quick-Start promised to speed up TCP, but only some applications benefited, and the speedup was small compared to simpler endpoint-only improvements.
sections.eli5: If fixing the problem costs money and time, and the current system is working even if not perfectly, most operators will stick with what they have. The technique needs to be so much better that it pays for itself.

sections.title: Trust Models and Security
sections.content:
ICMP Source Quench allowed routers to tell sources to slow down, but endpoints did not trust routers enough to act on unauthenticated signals. Routers could forge these messages, creating a denial-of-service risk. Later, Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) provided a more robust mechanism, where routers mark packets rather than send out-of-band signals.

The RFC notes that trust is not binary. An endpoint can partially trust a router if the router includes enough information for the endpoint to verify that the router actually saw the packets in question. However, asking endpoints to trust intermediate nodes in an untrusted Internet is a difficult policy question that remains open.
sections.eli5: When a stranger tells you to change your plans, do you listen? Probably not. The same applies to routers and endpoints. Without trust, signals get ignored or exploited.

sections.title: Operational and Technical Barriers
sections.content:
Some path-aware techniques fail because they require changes to routers' data planes that conflict with high-speed forwarding. Routers are optimized for simple per-packet decisions ('fast paths'), but many path-aware techniques need deeper packet inspection or context-sensitive processing, diverting packets to slower processors.

Per-connection state in routers becomes expensive as connection counts grow. Modern networks use tunnels that appear as single connections to intermediate routers, masking the actual connection count and making per-flow state infeasible at scale.

Even when a technique is available, applications often don't know how to use it. The sockets API has no way for applications to signal their network path expectations to the transport layer.
sections.eli5: Fast routers are fast because they process every packet the same quick way. Asking them to think hard about each packet slows them down. And even if the tools exist, applications don't know how to ask for what they need.

sections.title: Thirteen Lessons for Future Research
sections.content:
The RFC identifies invariant lessons that should apply to any path-aware proposal: justifying deployment against the status quo, providing value to early adopters, paying for the technique, managing operational changes, and planning for failure. Other lessons are context-dependent: whether outperforming end-to-end mechanisms is realistic, how much state is acceptable, and whether the trust model is sustainable.

Two lessons are marked 'Not Now': endpoints trusting intermediate nodes, and intermediate nodes trusting endpoints, without cryptographic mechanisms for verification. The research group noted that broader Internet threat model questions were being debated elsewhere and that path-aware research should account for those changes.
sections.eli5: Some rules apply everywhere: you have to show it's worth the cost, you need to help the first people to try it, and you need a way to turn things off if they go wrong. Other rules depend on your specific idea.
